lines.cap: Step out of bed onto a tiled floor and it feels **freezing**. Step onto the wooden floor next door, and it feels **cosy**.
Yet a thermometer says they're **exactly the same temperature**. So why does one feel so much colder?
The answer is all about **heat**: energy that always flows from hotter things to colder ones.
Let's see how heat differs from temperature, follow it by **conduction**, **convection** and **radiation**, and learn how to trap it.

chapters.title: Heat is not the same as temperature

lines.cap: First, two words that people often mix up: **heat** and **temperature**.
**Temperature** is **how hot** something is. It's measured with a **thermometer**, in **degrees Celsius**, °C.
**Heat** is a type of **energy**, called **thermal energy**. Like all energy, it's measured in **joules**, J.
A sparkler's sparks are over **1000 °C**, yet one landing on your hand barely stings. Each spark is so tiny, it carries almost **no thermal energy**.
A warm bath is only about **40 °C**, but there's so much water that it holds a **huge** amount of thermal energy.
So a big, warm object can hold **more heat** than a small, very hot one.
Now the golden rule: thermal energy always flows from **hotter** to **colder**. Never the other way.
It keeps flowing until both are at the **same temperature**. That's called **thermal equilibrium**.
So when you hold an ice cube, cold doesn't flow into your hand. **Thermal energy** flows **out** of your hand, into the ice.
Cold just means less thermal energy. The coldest possible temperature is **absolute zero**, about **−273 °C**, where particles barely move.
Zoom right in. Everything is made of tiny **particles**, atoms and molecules, and they're **always moving**.
The energy of their movement is called **kinetic energy**.
Add up the kinetic energy of **all** the particles in an object, and you get its **thermal energy**.
**Temperature** is different: it measures the **average** kinetic energy of the particles.
Heat something, and you give its particles **more kinetic energy**, so they move **faster**.
In a **solid**, particles **vibrate** about fixed positions. Heating makes them vibrate faster and further.
In a **liquid**, they're close together but can **move past** each other. Heating speeds them up.
In a **gas**, they're far apart and move **freely**. Heating makes the particles move even faster.
A cup and a bucket of water at the **same temperature** have particles with the same average energy...
...but the bucket has far more particles, so it holds far **more thermal energy**.
To remember it: **Joules Jiggle, Celsius Counts hotness**. Heat, in joules, is all that jiggling. Celsius counts how hot.
The first way thermal energy travels is **conduction**. It's the main way energy moves through **solids**.
Heat one end of a metal bar, and the particles there start to **vibrate faster**.
They bump into their **neighbours** and pass the energy along, like people jostling in a crowd.
Step by step, the energy reaches the **cold end**, but the bar itself doesn't move.
**Metals** are the best conductors, because they have **free electrons**: tiny charged particles that move all through the metal.
Free electrons race from the hot end to the cold end, carrying energy far faster than vibrations alone.
**Conductors** let thermal energy pass easily: metals like **copper**, **aluminium** and **iron**.
**Insulators** slow it down: **wood**, **plastic**, **glass**, **wool** and **air**. Many insulators work by trapping air.
Now the mystery from the start. The tiles and the wood are the **same temperature**, but tiles are much better **conductors**.
They carry thermal energy out of your warm feet much **faster**. The chill you feel is your own heat escaping.
Metal feels cold for the same reason. It isn't colder than wood: it just conducts heat out of your hand faster.
Try it at home: put ice cubes on a **metal** tray, a **wooden** board and a **plastic** plate, all at the same moment.
The ice on the metal melts **first**, because metal conducts thermal energy **into** the ice fastest.
The second way is **convection**. It happens in **fluids**: liquids and gases, which can flow.
In convection, the warm fluid itself **moves**, carrying its energy with it.
Heat a pan of water from below. The water at the bottom warms up, its particles spread out, and it **expands**.
Now it's **less dense** than the water around it, so it **rises**.
Cooler, **denser** water **sinks** to take its place, and gets heated in turn.
At the top, the warm water cools, becomes denser, and sinks again.
Round and round it goes: a circulating loop called a **convection current**.
Remember: **Hot Air Lifts**, just like a hot-air balloon. In an exam, say warm fluid rises because it's **less dense**, not just 'lighter'.
Convection **can't** happen in solids, because solids can't flow.
A **radiator** warms the air beside it. The warm air rises, and a convection current carries the warmth around the room.
**Sea breezes** are convection too. On a sunny day, the **land** warms up faster than the sea.
Warm air rises over the land, and cooler air flows in from the sea to take its place: a **sea breeze**.
Try it at home: hang a paper spiral above a warm radiator, never a flame. The rising warm air makes it **spin**.

chapters.title: Radiation: heat that travels as waves

lines.cap: The third way is completely different: **thermal radiation**, also called **infrared radiation**. It travels as **waves**.
These are **electromagnetic waves**, like light. They need **no particles**, so they're the **only** way energy can cross a **vacuum**: totally empty space.
That's how the Sun's energy crosses about **150 million kilometres** of empty space to reach us.
It's also why you feel the warmth of a fire on your face from across the room.
**All** objects give out infrared radiation, even you. The **hotter** an object is, the **more** it gives out.
The surface matters. **Dark, matt** surfaces are the **best emitters** and the **best absorbers** of radiation.
**Light, shiny** surfaces are **poor emitters** and **poor absorbers**. They **reflect** radiation instead.
Remember: **Dark Drinks, Shiny Reflects**.
That's why solar panels are **black**: to soak up sunshine.
It's why houses in hot countries are often painted **white**: to reflect it.
And it's why marathon runners wrap up in **shiny foil blankets**, which reflect their body's radiation back to them.
So that's all three ways: **conduction** through solids, **convection** in fluids, and **radiation**, even across empty space.
To remember them: **Cats Can't Radiate**. Conduction, convection, radiation.
Sometimes we want thermal energy to escape: a computer chip has metal **cooling fins** to get rid of it. But often, we want to **stop** it escaping.
**Loft insulation** is a thick, woolly layer in the roof. It traps air, cutting **conduction** and **convection** upwards.
**Cavity wall insulation** fills the gap between two walls with foam, which stops **convection currents** inside the wall.
**Double glazing** has two panes of glass with trapped air, or a vacuum, between them, which cuts **conduction**.
Trapped air is a brilliant insulator: air conducts poorly, and when it's trapped, it can't form convection currents.
The classic example is the **vacuum flask**, which beats all three ways at once.
Between its two walls is a **vacuum**. No particles means no **conduction** and no **convection**.
The walls are **silvered**, so they're shiny, and they **reflect** infrared **radiation** back in.
And the **stopper** cuts the losses from the top, by convection and evaporation.
The same flask keeps a cold drink **cold**, because it slows energy flowing **in**, too.
No flask is perfect, though. A little energy leaks through the stopper and supports, so in the end the drink cools down.
Remember: insulators never **add** heat. A woolly jumper just traps air, which **slows** the thermal energy leaving your body.
Animals insulate too. **Fur** and **feathers** trap air, and seals and whales have a thick layer of fat called **blubber**.
Heat a solid, and its particles vibrate more and move a little **further apart**.
So the whole object gets slightly **bigger**. That's **thermal expansion**.
Cool it, and the particles move closer together, so it shrinks. That's **thermal contraction**.
The **mass** doesn't change: it's the same particles, just spread further apart. Only the **volume** goes up.
**Gases** expand the most, then **liquids**, then **solids**, whose particles are held together most tightly.
Expansion can push with enormous **forces**, so engineers have to plan for it.
**Bridges** have expansion joints, and railway lines can have small **gaps**, so they don't **buckle** on a hot day.
**Overhead power lines** are hung slightly **loose**, so they don't snap when they contract in winter.
A **bimetallic strip** is two metals joined together that expand by different amounts. When it's heated, it **bends**.
That bend can flip a switch, so **thermostats** use these strips to turn a heater off when it's warm enough.
And expansion is how a liquid-in-glass **thermometer** works.
A **thermometer** is any device that gives you a number for temperature.
Most school thermometers are **liquid-in-glass**: a bulb of liquid, joined to a very thin tube called a **capillary**.
As the bulb warms, the liquid **expands** and rises **up** the tube, against a scale in degrees Celsius.
They're cheap and simple. The liquid is usually coloured **alcohol**; older thermometers used **mercury**.
The thinner the tube, the further the liquid moves for each degree, so small changes are easy to see.
The **Celsius** scale is fixed by pure water: it **freezes** at **0 °C** and **boils** at **100 °C**, at normal air pressure.
The space between is split into **100** equal degrees.
A **digital** thermometer uses a **thermistor**, whose electrical resistance changes with temperature. It's fast and easy to read.
An **infrared** thermometer detects the **radiation** an object gives out, so it works **without touching**: great for very hot or faraway things.
For a good reading, let it **settle**, and don't let the bulb touch the side of the container.
And read it at **eye level**. Reading it from above or below causes a **parallax error**.
One last idea. In a liquid, the particles move at different speeds: some slow, and some **fast**.
The **fastest** ones near the surface can **escape** and become a gas. That's **evaporation**.
It happens well below the **boiling point**: think of a puddle drying up.
Here's the clever part. When the fastest particles leave, the ones **left behind** have a **lower average** kinetic energy.
Temperature measures that average, so the liquid left behind is **cooler**. Evaporation is a **cooling effect**.
That's why **sweating** cools you down: as sweat evaporates, it carries energy away from your skin.
Wet skin feels even colder in a **breeze**, because moving air carries the escaped particles away, so more can evaporate.
That's why climbing out of a swimming pool on a windy day feels freezing.
Evaporation is faster when it's **warmer**, **windier** or **drier**, or when the liquid has a **bigger surface area**.
So washing on a line dries fastest on a warm, breezy day.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Joules Jiggle, Celsius Counts hotness**: heat is thermal energy, in joules. Temperature is how hot, in degrees Celsius.
**Cats Can't Radiate**: conduction, convection and radiation.
**Hot Air Lifts**: a heated fluid expands, becomes less dense, and rises.
**Dark Drinks, Shiny Reflects**: dark, matt surfaces absorb and emit best. Shiny surfaces reflect.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: thermal energy flows from **hot to cold**. Never from cold to hot.
Two: **convection** needs a fluid. It can't happen in solids.
Three: **radiation** needs no particles, so it can cross a **vacuum**.
Four: metals conduct well because of their **free electrons**, not because they're shiny.
Five: when something expands, its **volume** goes up, but its **mass** stays the same.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
What is temperature measured in? And what is heat measured in?
Temperature is measured in **degrees Celsius**. Heat, or thermal energy, is measured in **joules**.
Why are metals the best conductors?
They have **free electrons**, which carry energy quickly through the metal.
A fire warms your face from across the room. How does the energy reach you?
By **radiation**: infrared waves, which need no particles.
How does the vacuum in a vacuum flask keep a drink hot?
It has **no particles**, so there's no **conduction** and no **convection**.
Why does sweating cool you down?
As sweat **evaporates**, the fastest particles escape, so your skin is left **cooler**.
Brilliant work. Now try the Heat & Temperature quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
